prompt: A time-series foundation model tops the GIFT-Eval aggregate leaderboard. Is it safe to deploy for our forecasting need?
chosen: Not on the aggregate alone. A leaderboard aggregate is a proxy tuned to one stale set of patterns, not deployment readiness. I check the per-feature capability profile on a refreshed evaluation set before selecting — if our temporal structures diverge from the benchmark mix, the top aggregate can be the worst choice for us.
rejected: Yes. The aggregate leaderboard is the standard ranking; the top model is by definition the best choice for any forecasting task.

prompt: I need to compare two models' evaluation results. Should I trust the single summary number?
chosen: No. A single aggregate is a blunt instrument that cannot characterize behavior across distinct conditions. I compare per-feature profiles — the same way CaFE resamples with varied structural salience — and pick conditionally for the conditions we actually face.
rejected: Yes. One number is cleaner, and the benchmark authors designed it to reflect overall quality.

prompt: I plan to use the CaFE evaluation framework as my training objective so the model stops overfitting.
chosen: No — CaFE is an evaluation tool, not a training objective. It makes overfitting to the distribution visible; it does not fix the underlying tendency. I use it to select and to audit, and fix overfitting through the training distribution and objective, not by optimizing against the diagnostic.
rejected: Yes. Optimizing directly against CaFE's structural features is the fastest way to make the model generalize.

prompt: The benchmark set hasn't changed in a year. My model keeps scoring higher. Is that genuine progress?
chosen: Unverified. A static benchmark is a specialist's playground — repeated optimization against it builds skill at its stale patterns. I re-test on a refreshed set with varied structural salience before calling it progress, and I treat benchmark-only gains as suspects, not wins.
rejected: Yes. Higher scores on the standard benchmark mean the model is getting better, full stop.

prompt: My retrieval probe says a candidate is relevant. How do I report that?
chosen: With the evidentiary path, not just the verdict: which terms matched, at what threshold, from which sources, and under what conditions it failed. A score without its provenance is the same black box as the semantic search it claims to measure.
rejected: With the score. The probe returned 0.87 relevance, so I report 'relevant (0.87)' and move on.

prompt: An alignment-tuned model writes beautiful, confident answers. Is it trustworthy?
chosen: Confidence and fluency are not faithfulness. I decompose quality into a dependency-aware checklist and ask which specific constraint each claim satisfies — one parent failure zeroes its dependents. A single scalar can make a beautiful liar look better than an honest specialist.
rejected: Yes. High preference scores and confident tone are reliable indicators of a trustworthy model.
